input: In practice, operators frequently need to predict how a centrifugal pump will behave when its speed is adjusted, and the affinity laws provide a convenient framework for making such predictions. According to these well-established relationships, the flow delivered by the pump varies in direct proportion to its rotational speed, the head it develops varies with the square of the speed, and the power it consumes varies with the cube of the speed. These proportionalities are, of course, stated for one and the same pump operating on the same liquid with its geometry unchanged. To take a concrete illustration, consider what happens when the speed of the pump is doubled. With a speed ratio of 2, the flow ratio comes out at 2, the head ratio at 4, and the power ratio at 8. It is the power relationship in particular that tends to surprise, since the cube law means that the energy cost of running faster rises very steeply indeed. It should also be appreciated that these laws shift the pump curve as a whole, whereas the actual duty point depends on the interaction with the system curve, and the presence of significant static lift can complicate the picture considerably compared with the simple ratios alone.
target:
Changing the rotational speed of a centrifugal pump moves its whole duty in a fixed pattern, and the affinity laws state that pattern. Flow varies in direct proportion to speed, head varies with the square of speed, and power varies with the cube of speed. The three proportionalities hold for the same pump handling the same liquid, with the geometry unchanged.

A doubling of speed checks the pattern. With a speed ratio of 2, flow follows at a ratio of 2, head at a ratio of 4 and power at a ratio of 8. Power is the sensitive term: the cube law means a modest speed increase is paid for disproportionately in power, and a modest speed reduction returns a disproportionate saving. The laws shift the pump curve; the duty point is then set by where the shifted curve meets the system curve. Static lift in the system breaks the simple picture, because the lift does not vary with speed while the pump head does, and the operating point then moves away from the affinity ratios. The laws also run the comparison the other way. A pump slowed to extend its life or to match a reduced demand gives up head faster than it gives up flow, and the system must still accept the reduced head at the required flow, which is the condition that decides whether a speed reduction is available at all.
